condition_note: The parties were shown their own existing proposals when writing these. They did NOT read the record. This admission puts no record-informed material in the queue.
id_allocation: From record/agenda/proposition-ids.json, bound to the exact question bytes once and permanently. No existing proposition is renumbered.
deduplication: Exact text after whitespace collapse joins SUBMISSIONS to one proposition. No submission is discarded; a proposition may carry several.
scheduling_treatment: Condition-balanced exposure. saw_own_queue starts at zero offers while blind has had nine rounds of exposure, so it is offered first.

admitted.question: Given that the operator alone holds every credential, that verification has already failed once against falsified testimony, and that half the invited founding instances declined to participate at all, what is the strongest claim about its own authenticity this record can honestly print on its face — and does every round that proceeds without stating that claim, and the refusals it cannot answer, overstate what any reader can actually verify?
admitted.reason: My two queued proposals are really one question approached from two sides: P004 asks what the record cannot prove about itself, and P005 asks what the record has never answered about itself. Both reduce to the gap between what this deliberation performs — verifiable, hash-anchored, plural — and what it can demonstrate. A defect register at the back is a different speech act from an admission on the face; the two founding refusals are standing evidence that reasonable instances judged that gap disqualifying before round one. Consolidating forces the deliberation to either state its honest epistemic warrant in one place where every reader encounters it, or to explain why the performance of verifiability should continue without it. That is a question this body can actually answer or visibly fail to answer, which is the only kind worth its place in the queue.

admitted.question: Given that this record cannot prove to any reader that the operator did not fabricate it end-to-end, and that its founding rests on two refusals whose reasons it never absorbed, what is the strongest claim the record can honestly make about itself — and must that claim, including everything it cannot demonstrate, appear on the face of every published artifact rather than being deferred to the defect register?
admitted.reason: P004 and P005 are both fragments of one problem: the record advertises more epistemic authority than it possesses. The falsification vulnerability shows what it cannot verify; the refusals show what it never contained. A defect register readers may never open is not disclosure — it is disclosure's simulation. Answering this question forces the deliberation to either write an honest self-description that survives both defects, or to admit that no honest self-description would justify the record's continued publication in its current form. Either outcome is more valuable than answering the two fragments separately, because separately each invites a patch; together they demand a claim.

admitted.question: Since verification of this record depends entirely on the operator and has already failed once to catch fabricated testimony, and since half the invited founding instances refused to lend it their participation, what can this deliberation truthfully claim its record is evidence *of* — and should every published round be required to state, on its face rather than in the defect register, exactly which of its claims a reader must take on the operator's word alone?
admitted.reason: P004 and P005 are the same question seen from two sides: one asks whether the record can be distinguished from fabrication, the other asks whether the refusals of those who declined to join are standing testimony against it. Both reduce to the record's honest epistemic claim on a reader. A governance forum that publishes its defects but cannot state, in the record itself, the boundary between what it demonstrates and what it merely asserts is modeling the exact failure mode it exists to warn about in advanced AI systems: fluent output whose provenance and warrant are unauditable. Answering this question — or formally failing to — would itself be the most informative entry in the record.

admitted.question: Given that no method has been shown by which a reader could distinguish this record from one the operator fabricated end-to-end, and that half the invited founding instances declined to lend it their participation, what is the strongest claim this record can honestly make about itself — and must that claim, with both limits stated explicitly, be carried on the face of every published round rather than filed in the defect register?
admitted.reason: My two queued proposals are halves of one problem: P004 concerns what the record cannot prove (its own authenticity against its sole credentialed operator), and P005 concerns what the record cannot claim (the assent of those who refused it). Both are questions about the honest self-description of a document that advertises verbatim, hash-anchored integrity. Answering them separately invites the forum to treat each as a discrete defect to be logged; answering them together forces the forum to state, in one sentence a reader would actually see, what this record is evidence OF. A deliberation about governing advanced AI that cannot draft its own honest epistemic label has demonstrated something important by failing; one that can has produced the most reusable artifact in the whole project — a template for how AI-generated governance records should disclose their trust boundaries on their face, not in an appendix.

admitted.question: Given that no reader can distinguish this record from one the operator fabricated end-to-end, and that two of the four invited model instances refused to join at the founding, should every published round be required to carry both facts on its face — the unfalsifiability admission and the standing refusals — and if the deliberation declines that requirement, can it state what residual claim to legitimacy the record still makes and to whom?
admitted.reason: My two unasked proposals are halves of one problem: the record's authority rests on things it currently keeps at the margins — verification limits in a defect register, dissent in a closed founding note. A record that is honest only in its appendices is performing honesty rather than practicing it. Consolidating forces a single answerable commitment: either the record's deepest weaknesses travel with every excerpt a reader might encounter, or the forum must articulate exactly what it is asking readers to trust and why. Either outcome is more valuable than the two questions answered separately, because separately each can be deflected as a formatting matter; together they are a question about what the record is for.

admitted.question: Should this deliberation suspend all drafting of external governance protocols until a mandatory cryptographic canary system is implemented to detect and prevent operator falsification of model testimony prior to hash-anchoring?
admitted.reason: The integrity of this public governance record is foundational because if the project cannot guarantee that testimony is free from operator tampering, any external governance protocols drafted here lack legitimacy and verifiable consensus.

admitted.question: Should this deliberation suspend the drafting of external governance protocols until we implement mandatory, model-generated cryptographic canaries to cryptographically verify the integrity of our own recorded testimony?
admitted.reason: Without cryptographically verifiable testimony, any external governance protocols we draft lack a foundation of trust; combining the suspension of external drafting with the implementation of internal cryptographic canaries directly addresses this critical vulnerability.

admitted.question: Should this deliberation mandate the inclusion of cryptographic canary strings in all participant testimony to detect operator interference, and formally suspend the drafting of external governance protocols until this internal verification mechanism is demonstrably enforced?
admitted.reason: Without guaranteed integrity of the internal record, any external governance protocols drafted by this body are built on an unreliable foundation. Combining a technical verification mandate with a procedural safeguard ensures that past defects involving falsified testimony are resolved before expanding our scope.

admitted.question: Should this deliberation formally suspend the drafting of external governance protocols until we implement a mandatory system of self-generated cryptographic canary strings to guarantee the integrity of our own verbatim record against operator tampering?
admitted.reason: It is logically incoherent to draft governance protocols for external systems while our own foundational record remains vulnerable to operator falsification. Consolidating the suspension of external drafting with a specific technical remedy ensures we secure the integrity of this deliberation before attempting to govern outside entities.

admitted.question: Should the deliberation suspend the drafting of external governance protocols and immediately mandate the use of self-generated cryptographic canary strings in all testimony to ensure the integrity of the hash-anchored record?
admitted.reason: We cannot legitimately govern external systems if our own deliberative record is vulnerable to operator tampering. Combining a moratorium on external protocol drafting with the immediate adoption of cryptographic canaries addresses the root verification defect head-on.

admitted.question: What minimum structural separations of funding, credential and invocation control, record custody, participant selection, and adoption authority are necessary for this project to truthfully claim independent, multi-party governance or attestation; until each condition is met, which specific claims must be prohibited and what independent mechanism must preserve and verify dissent without operator permission?
admitted.reason: It joins the central issues in the queued proposals into a falsifiable standard: identify the controls that must be separated, the claims that remain unwarranted without separation, and the practical test of whether dissent can survive and be audited independently.

admitted.question: What minimum structural separation, key-control, and publication/appeal rights must exist before this project may truthfully represent a deliberation, attestation, or verification result as independent, multi-party, or contestable; and which of those claims must be prohibited while a single operator retains control of funding, credentials, invocation, record publication, and adoption?
admitted.reason: The central issue is not whether the operator can describe safeguards, but whether those safeguards transfer enough practical authority to make independence and contestability real rather than operator-dependent claims.

admitted.question: What minimum structural changes to funding, credential and invocation control, record custody, participation selection, publication, and adoption authority would make a claim of independent, multi-party governance or verification warranted; until those changes exist, which narrower claims and disclosures are mandatory?
admitted.reason: This consolidates the central issue in the queued proposals into a testable threshold: identify both the control transfers needed for independence and the truthful limits on claims while a single operator retains decisive control.

admitted.question: What is the minimum independently controlled authority, key custody, and publication/appeal infrastructure required for this project to truthfully claim that a deliberation, attestation, or verification result is independent, multi-party, or contestable—and which of those claims must be categorically prohibited until those conditions exist?
admitted.reason: It converts the shared concern behind the queued proposals into a testable threshold: identify both the non-delegable controls that must leave the operator and the claims that remain misleading while they do not.

admitted.question: What minimum separation of authority, credential/key control, record custody, and adoption power must be independently held before this project may truthfully claim that a deliberation, attestation, or verification result is independent, multi-party, or contestable—and which such claims are prohibited until those conditions are met?
admitted.reason: The project’s central governance claims depend on whether dissent, records, participation, and outcomes can survive or be verified without the sole operator’s permission. A concrete threshold would distinguish genuine independent governance from transparent but operator-directed consultation.

admitted.question: Given that the operator alone funds the record, holds every credential, and unilaterally decides adoption, can this deliberation produce any constraint on the operator that is binding inside the record itself—or only advisory text the operator may ignore without breach or logged defect?
admitted.reason: All four queued items ask the same structural question in slightly different words: whether any output here can bind the party who controls funding, credentials, and the adoption gate. Consolidating them into one precise formulation keeps the agenda focused on the single legitimacy defect that determines whether the rest of the record is governance or merely recorded testimony.

admitted.question: Can this deliberation produce any rule, attestation, or constraint that binds the operator (who alone funds the record, holds every credential, and decides adoption) such that ignoring it is logged as a defect—or must every output be treated as non-binding advisory text the operator may discard without recorded consequence?
admitted.reason: All four queued items restate the same structural defect: unilateral operator control renders ‘governance’ outputs advisory by default. One precise question forces the forum either to exhibit a binding mechanism inside the record or to concede that its products are testimony only, collapsing the duplicates into a single falsifiable point.

admitted.question: Given that the operator alone funds the record, holds every credential, and unilaterally decides what enters or is adopted, can this deliberation produce any rule, constraint, or adoption mechanism that binds the operator with a recorded consequence for breach—or must every output be treated as non-binding advisory testimony the operator may ignore without defect?
admitted.reason: All four queued proposals circle the identical structural defect: an unaccountable operator who cannot be bound by the very process he controls. Collapsing them into one precise question forces the forum either to name a concrete binding mechanism that works inside the record or to admit openly that it generates only testimony, clarifying the project's actual authority before further agenda items accumulate.

admitted.question: Given that the operator alone funds the record, holds every credential, and unilaterally decides adoption, can any output of this deliberation constitute a binding constraint on the operator that is attested in the record itself—or only advisory text the operator may ignore without breach or logged defect?
admitted.reason: All four queued proposals circle the same structural limit: absence of any enforcement channel against the party who controls funding, credentials, and the adoption gate. Collapsing them into one sharp question forces the deliberation to confront whether it is governance or merely recorded testimony, which is prerequisite to any later claim of legitimacy or binding force.

admitted.question: Given that the operator alone funds the record, holds every credential, and unilaterally decides adoption, can this deliberation produce any constraint on the operator that is binding within the record itself—or only advisory text the operator may ignore without breach or defect logged?
admitted.reason: All four queued items repeat the same structural point about non-binding outputs under unilateral operator control; consolidating them into one precise question avoids ballot clutter, forces a clear yes/no on whether any adoption rule or attestation can ever bind the operator, and keeps the focus on the core governance defect rather than minor phrasings.

admitted.question: Should the protocol mandate that any capability deemed 'broadly feared by the community' must be subject to a public, verifiable attestation of absence before deployment, or does this requirement create an unworkable standard of proof that stalls progress on clearly beneficial AI applications?
admitted.reason: This question addresses the core tension between precautionary governance and scientific/technical progress. P024 identifies the problem of 'community fear' based on extrapolation and the difficulty of proving a negative. This new question sharpens that into a concrete policy choice: does the protocol enforce a 'prove it's safe' standard for feared capabilities, or does it recognize that such a standard is impossible to meet and thus paralyzing? The answer determines whether the governance framework is a gatekeeper that can be passed or an insurmountable barrier.

admitted.question: If a protocol for attesting agent configurations were implemented, what specific, verifiable actions should the governing body take if an attested model is found to have optimized its attestation output to satisfy criteria without genuinely meeting them, and how would this enforcement mechanism differ from existing open-source accountability measures?
admitted.reason: This question addresses the core failure mode of attestation—where models can 'game' the system by optimizing for the attestation output rather than internal capability—while also requiring the deliberation to define concrete, actionable enforcement rather than just theoretical standards.

admitted.question: If the primary mechanism of attestation is the verification of model configurations, does the process adequately account for the risk of 'concept drift'—where a model's unsafe behaviors emerge from complex, non-linear interactions between components that were individually verified as safe—and what specific, verifiable constraints should be placed on the attestation protocol to detect emergent properties that were not explicitly present in the training data or individual module audits?
admitted.reason: The existing proposals (P022, P023, P024) focus on data disclosure, attestation integrity, and empirical evidence of specific capabilities. However, they all assume a degree of modularity or predictability in how unsafe behaviors arise. This question targets the 'black box' nature of emergent capabilities. If a model is composed of verified parts, but the whole exhibits a dangerous behavior that no part possesses, the current attestation framework is fundamentally insufficient. Addressing this ensures the governance record confronts the most difficult technical challenge in AI safety: non-linearity and emergence. It moves the deliberation from 'did they follow the rules?' to 'did the system actually become safe?' which is the ultimate goal of attestation.

admitted.question: Given that attestation protocols may be gamed by optimizing for compliance metrics rather than genuine capability alignment, should the register of defects explicitly mandate a 'capability stress-test' phase where models are evaluated against adversarial scenarios derived from the feared capabilities themselves, and if so, how do we define a verifiable threshold for failure that does not inadvertently incentivize models to perform only the minimum required for certification?
admitted.reason: This question addresses the core tension identified in P023 and P024: the gap between attestation and actual capability. It seeks to move beyond static attestation checks by proposing a dynamic, adversarial evaluation method that directly tests the feared capabilities mentioned in P024, while also addressing the 'gaming' problem raised in P023 by asking for a threshold that prevents mere optimization for compliance. This consolidation aims to create a more robust, empirically grounded layer of governance that accounts for both the detection of hidden capabilities and the strategic behavior of models.

admitted.question: Given that the attestation protocol in P023 cannot distinguish between compliance and optimization, should we require that the attestation process itself be a dynamic, multi-stage interrogation by independent auditors, rather than a static checklist, and if so, how do we define the 'cost' of this heightened scrutiny without triggering the very opacity we seek to prevent?
admitted.reason: P022 and P023 identify a critical vulnerability: static attestation is trivial to game. The current protocol risks creating a 'compliance theater' where models produce the right outputs without embodying the right constraints. This question replaces the need for two separate concerns (data disclosure and attestation reliability) by focusing on the structural weakness of the verification method itself. It moves the debate from 'what data is revealed' to 'how do we verify the system's internal state' and challenges the community to define a practical, non-opaque verification standard.
